vignette:
Kwame is a 20-year-old African American doctor who served a tour as a combat medic in Afghanistan. The trauma that reshaped his life occurred during a rocket-propelled grenade attack on his forward operating base’s aid station. He had been treating a soldier with a chest wound when the blast hit. The room filled with smoke; he could not catch his breath as he dragged the soldier to cover. Then, for a few seconds, an unnatural silence fell—no shouts, no gunfire, only the ringing in his ears. He saw a colleague’s body torn apart by shrapnel. Those moments—the breathlessness, the silence, the raw violence—became the template for his fear.

After returning home, Kwame completed his residency and now works in a busy urban emergency department. But the memories of that day do not come easily. He finds himself pushing the memory away before he can fully recall it, as if his mind slams a door shut. What does surface arrives in disconnected pieces: the smell of smoke, the weight of the soldier, the silence, but never a coherent story. There are entire seconds he cannot retrieve no matter how hard he tries, leaving him with gaps that feel like missing teeth in a smile.

Those gaps and fragments have eroded his sense of self. Kwame feels he no longer knows who he is—the confident healer who once believed hard work and skill could protect anyone has been replaced by a stranger who startles at his own reflection. His beliefs about the world are shattered; he now sees danger everywhere, even in the sterile hallways of the hospital. He has come to believe that he must be on guard all the time, scanning every room, every silence, every pause in conversation for a threat.

That hypervigilance is what first connects his negative appraisals to his triggers. Because he feels he must always watch for danger, he notices the smallest changes in his breathing. A moment of breathlessness after climbing two flights of stairs—something he would have dismissed before—now floods him with alarm and a wave of shattered beliefs: *This is how it starts. The world is not safe.* Similarly, sudden silence in the emergency department, when the monitors go quiet and the staff pauses, sends his heart racing. The silence feels like the seconds before the rocket hit, and with it comes the conviction that he has lost the person he used to be.

These triggers, in turn, reinforce his negative appraisals. Each time breathlessness or silence catches him off guard, he is reminded that he is not the same person, that his world is unstable. The cycle tightens: because he sees himself as fundamentally altered, he feels he cannot trust his own memory. When a fragmented piece of the trauma surfaces—a flash of smoke, a scream—he immediately pushes it away, because to fully remember would mean confronting a self he no longer recognizes. That active suppression creates more gaps, and the gaps themselves feed his sense of identity loss. Moreover, the act of pushing memory away is itself a physiological stressor; he sometimes finds himself short of breath after forcing the memory down, creating a new somatic trigger out of his own avoidance.

At work, the violence of the trauma is triggered most starkly. When a gunshot victim is wheeled in, Kwame’s mind floods with disconnected images of his colleague’s body. He stiffens, his breathing shallow. The memory of that moment—though he cannot retrieve a full narrative—convinces him that his beliefs about safety are right: violence is everywhere. He then becomes even more hypervigilant, scanning the trauma bay for any sign of further threat, which makes him more sensitive to the next silence or breathlessness.

Over months, this mutual reinforcement has narrowed his world. He avoids conversations about the military, but more subtly he finds himself leaving the room whenever the emergency department grows quiet. He has started taking the elevator instead of the stairs to avoid feeling breathless. A senior colleague noticed he seemed distant during critical resuscitations, and his once-steady hands now tremble during suturing. Kwame knows something is wrong but has been terrified that seeking help would mean admitting he has lost himself permanently. What finally brought him to the clinic was a small moment: during a code blue, the team fell silent for two seconds while the defibrillator charged, and Kwame felt as though he was back in the smoking aid station, unable to breathe. He walked out mid-resuscitation—the first time he has ever abandoned a patient. Now he sits in the therapist’s office, hoping to reclaim the person he was, but afraid that who he has become is all that remains.
